meta.theme: an idea followed from the oil leases that produced it to the maxim it became: the original account needs a value common to all bidders, estimates erring in both directions and an award to the highest number, and in its travelled form it keeps only the warning, becoming a claim no outcome can contradict while the conditions that made it usable stay behind

meta.reviewer_notes: The passage is built so that the psychological reading is available at every point and refuted at two: the estimates err in both directions, and the remedy is a subtraction rather than a change of temperament. The charity book supplies the counter-case that separates a common value from a private one, and the EXCEPT item's false option is the popular generalisation rather than a detail, so that the three true options come one from each of the other readings. 2026-10-03 CAT-size pass: 572→572 words, 5→5 paragraphs, 5→4 questions. Dropped q2 (except on p4, resting on the same first removal that comparative q4 tests directly); why_difficult no longer ties each removal to a question of its own.

quality.adversarial_review: Three rivals hold one option in each of the five questions. The first is the overpricing reading: competitive sale produces prices above value, so a winning bid is evidence of error. The passage concedes the observed shortfall and then removes the conclusion with the charity book, where the highest bidder has nothing to have overpaid against, and with the closing point that a bidder who subtracts can win and still pay less than the tract is worth. The second, and the live rival, is the psychological reading, on which excitement and overconfidence raise bids: it is attractive because the first paragraph reports bidders resenting the explanation, and it is killed twice, by the statement that the geologists' errors ran in both directions and cancelled, and by a remedy that is a subtraction rather than a discipline. The third is the generalising reading, on which any contest awarded to the most optimistic judgement produces the same curse; it is refused by the sentence that removes the first condition and watches the result disappear, and it is the false option in the EXCEPT item. The comparative question's near-tie is the number of bidders, which the passage does mention as a reason to shade further, and which is not what separates the tract from the book. (2026-10-03, CAT-size pass: q2 was dropped, so any note above about it no longer applies.)

passage.title: The Leases on the Gulf Coast

paragraphs.text: In the middle of the last century the engineers of an oil company on the Gulf coast noticed something about the leases their firm had won at auction. The tracts were returning less than the company's own geologists had forecast, and not occasionally but as a rule. The obvious explanations were tried and put aside. The geologists were not incompetent, since their assessments of tracts the firm failed to win were no worse. They were not systematically extravagant either: taken over all the tracts they examined, their errors ran in both directions and cancelled.

The account that survived is arithmetical and says nothing about character. Suppose several firms bid for a tract whose true value, whatever it may be, is the same for all of them, and suppose each forms an honest estimate as likely to fall below that value as above it. The estimates are then a scatter around the truth. An auction, however, does not sell to a bidder drawn at random from the scatter. It sells to the highest, which is to say to whichever firm's error ran furthest upward. The winner is selected for optimism rather than convicted of it, and the remedy is a subtraction: shade the bid below the estimate, and shade it further when the bidders are many and when the dispersion of their estimates is wide.

The idea was resented before it was adopted. Bidders told that their victories were a tax on enthusiasm heard an accusation of folly, which was the one thing the explanation had been constructed to avoid. Within twenty years it was standard, taught to anybody who would ever seal an envelope, and the phrase had begun to travel. It left the oil fields for the sale room, and the sale room for general conversation, where it hardened into a maxim: the winner has overpaid. Take-over battles, transfer fees, the advances paid for first novels, the salaries of chief executives: each is now explained, when it disappoints, by a curse that began as a remark about petroleum leases.

What travelled was the warning. What stayed behind were the conditions. The original account requires a value that is the same for every bidder, estimates that err in both directions, and a rule awarding the object to the highest number. Remove the first and the result disappears: at a charity auction a signed book is worth different amounts to different people, and whoever pays most is simply whoever wanted it most, with nothing to have overpaid against. Remove the second and a story about bias, not about scatter, is what is needed. Keep all three and the outcome is still not fixed, since a bidder who makes the subtraction can win the tract and pay less than it turns out to be worth.

This is why the travelled version is worse than useless. In that form no outcome can count against it. A buyer who does badly has been cursed; a buyer who does well was lucky; a bidder who withdraws was wise. A warning nobody can fail to satisfy tells nobody what to do. The narrow version tells them a great deal: it names three conditions a person about to bid can check in an afternoon, and an amount to take off when the three hold. The part of the idea that travelled was never of any use, and the part left behind is the whole of what was found out.

questions.target_mistake: taking the passage for an endorsement or a debunking of the curse itself, when its subject is what happened to the idea between its origin and its current use
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say beforehand: the author follows one idea from the conditions that produced it to a popular form those conditions did not survive, and says which of the two is worth having.
questions.stem: The author's primary purpose in the passage is

options.A: to warn buyers that sale by competition reliably produces prices above what the object is worth
options.B: to explain an expensive and repeated failure of judgement by the psychology of competitive bidding
options.C: to follow an idea from the conditions that produced it to a popular form in which they are missing
options.D: to show that a result first established about auctions holds wherever the most hopeful judgement wins

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph opens with the passage's own statement of its subject: 'What travelled was the warning. What stayed behind were the conditions.' The paragraphs on either side of it are the two ends of that journey, one giving the original account and one judging the version now in circulation.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names that movement. The first two paragraphs establish where the idea came from and what it required; the third tracks its spread into a maxim; the fourth lists the conditions that did not spread; the fifth compares what each version can do for somebody about to bid. A purpose that settled whether the curse is real would leave the third and fifth paragraphs without work.
explanation.question_type_note: In a passage that traces the career of an idea, the purpose usually concerns the difference between two versions of it rather than the truth of either. Check that your option explains why the history is there.
explanation.reading_habit: When an essay follows a phrase out of the place it was invented, ask what was carried and what was dropped. That pair is almost always the point of the piece.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage grants the original observation about the leases and then removes the general warning twice over: a bidder who makes the subtraction can win and still pay less than the tract is worth, and where values are private the highest bidder has nothing to have overpaid against.
distractors.seductive_element: The opening reports a firm losing money on the auctions it won, which is exactly the evidence a warning of this kind would be built on.

distractors.why_wrong: The account offered is called arithmetical and is said to say nothing about character; the winner is 'selected for optimism rather than convicted of it'. The passage also records that bidders heard an accusation of folly, and notes that this was the one thing the explanation was built to avoid.
distractors.seductive_element: Losses that repeat invite a story about temperament, and the resentment of the bidders is described in detail, which puts psychology in the reader's mind.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the travelled version that the last two paragraphs exist to criticise. The passage states three conditions and shows the result disappearing when the first is removed, so what it establishes is a boundary rather than a general law about contests.
distractors.seductive_element: The third paragraph lists take-overs, transfer fees and executive pay, and a list of applications reads like a demonstration of reach rather than a specimen of overreach.

questions.target_mistake: supplying a psychological premise the account explicitly does without, or offering the observed loss, which is what the account has to explain rather than something it assumes
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: for the winner to be the most optimistic estimator, the size of a firm's bid has to follow the size of its estimate.
questions.stem: The explanation given in the second paragraph depends on the assumption that

options.A: a firm that assessed a tract more generously would, in general, offer more money for it
options.B: the sums the company paid for its leases were larger than the leases turned out to be worth
options.C: competition between rival bidders raises what each is prepared to pay above his own estimate
options.D: any procedure that selects the highest of several judgements will produce the same effect

explanation.expert_notice: The argument has a hidden hinge. It is stated in terms of estimates, the scatter, the error running furthest upward, but what the auction actually compares is money. Nothing in the paragraph says the two move together, and the conclusion collapses unless they do.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option supplies that link. If bids did not follow estimates, the highest bidder need not be the most optimistic assessor, and the winner would be drawn from the scatter in the way the paragraph denies. The assumption is required and unstated, which is what an assumption question asks for; it is also modest enough that the argument does not need any claim about how much more a generous assessor offers.
explanation.question_type_note: An assumption is a premise the argument needs and does not state. Test a candidate by denying it: if the conclusion still follows, it was not an assumption.
explanation.reading_habit: Watch for arguments that move between two quantities, a judgement and a price, a belief and a vote, and ask what has to be true for the second to track the first. That unstated link is where these questions live.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the fact the explanation was constructed to account for, reported in the first paragraph. An argument does not assume the thing it sets out to explain, and stating the outcome again supplies none of the reasoning that connects the scatter of estimates to the identity of the winner.
distractors.seductive_element: It is true, it is in the passage, and it sits so close to the conclusion that it can be mistaken for a premise rather than the puzzle.

distractors.why_wrong: The account is described as arithmetical and as saying nothing about character, and it works with bidders whose estimates err in both directions and who bid at or below them. A premise about competition inflating willingness to pay would replace the mechanism rather than support it.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the explanation most readers arrive holding, and the paragraph about resentful bidders keeps temperament in view.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph argues about one arrangement with three features, and the passage later shows the result vanishing when the values are private. A general claim about selecting the highest judgement is not needed for the argument and is denied by the example of the signed book.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like the abstract form of the same idea, and readers who like an argument tend to assume it assumes its own most general version.

questions.target_mistake: separating the two cases by the number of bidders or by the professionalism of the room, when the passage separates them by whether the object has one value or many
questions.stem: The signed book at a charity auction differs from an oil tract, in the author's account, in that

options.A: the tract was bought by a company that had to justify the price it paid, and the book by somebody who did not
options.B: the tract was fought over by professionals under pressure, while nobody in the charity room was competing hard
options.C: the tract had one value that was the same for every bidder, while the book was worth different amounts to each
options.D: the tract drew many more bidders than the book, so the highest of the estimates lay further from the truth

explanation.expert_notice: The book is introduced to remove exactly one thing. The fourth paragraph says 'Remove the first and the result disappears' and then gives the case: a signed book 'is worth different amounts to different people', so the buyer who pays most 'is simply whoever wanted it most'.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the difference the example was built to isolate. Where the value is common, the highest bid is the largest upward error about one quantity; where the value is private, the highest bid is the strongest preference, and there is no shared number it can be too high against. Every other feature of the two sales is left untouched by the passage, which is what makes this the comparison it draws.
explanation.question_type_note: When a passage introduces a second case to test a condition, the comparison being drawn is the condition itself. Ignore the incidental differences between the two settings.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask why the author chose this particular example rather than another. An example built to remove one condition will differ from the original in exactly that respect.

distractors.why_wrong: Accountability for a price appears nowhere in the passage, and it would not restore the curse if it did: what makes the highest charity bid innocent is that there is no common value for it to exceed, not the absence of anyone to answer to.
distractors.seductive_element: A company and a charity room differ in a dozen obvious ways, and this is the most businesslike of them.

distractors.why_wrong: Pressure and professionalism belong to the psychological account the passage sets aside in its second paragraph, where the explanation is called arithmetical and free of any claim about character. The example is chosen to vary the kind of value, and the passage says so.
distractors.seductive_element: Charity rooms really are more relaxed than oil auctions, so the contrast feels true even though the passage never draws it.

distractors.why_wrong: The number of bidders is a real part of the account, but it governs how much a bidder should subtract when the conditions hold rather than whether they hold at all. With a private value, adding bidders to the charity room produces more competition and still leaves nothing to have overpaid against.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the near-tie: the second paragraph does say to shade further when the bidders are many, so the reader has been handed a quantity that varies between the two cases.

questions.target_mistake: treating the curse as a verdict on every winner, when the passage makes it a correctable consequence of one arrangement
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: the remedy is a subtraction, so winning after the subtraction is possible and carries no implication of having paid too much.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A buyer who pays more than any rival was willing to pay has by that fact paid more than the object is worth.
options.B: A bidder who felt no excitement during a sale would have been unlikely to be caught by the curse at all.
options.C: A committee that appoints whichever candidate it rates most highly is making the mistake the bidders made.
options.D: A bidder who subtracts as the account advises may still win, and need not have paid too much when he does.

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph ends by refusing to make the outcome inevitable even with every condition in place: 'a bidder who makes the subtraction can win the tract and pay less than it turns out to be worth.' The remedy in the second paragraph is arithmetic, so it is available to anybody.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that sentence generalised one step. Since the winner's disadvantage comes from bidding the unadjusted estimate, a bidder who takes off the recommended amount is no longer the one whose error ran furthest upward in money; he wins when his adjusted figure is still the largest, which is compatible with paying below value. This is why the passage treats the curse as a correctable feature of an arrangement rather than a fate attached to winning.
explanation.question_type_note: Where a passage supplies a remedy, test every option against a bidder who has applied it. Options that make the result unavoidable contradict the existence of the remedy.
explanation.reading_habit: If an author gives both a mechanism and a correction, the inference on offer usually concerns the corrected case. Ask what the world looks like for somebody who has taken the advice.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the travelled maxim in its strongest form, and the charity book is the counter-case: whoever pays most for the signed book is whoever wanted it most, with nothing to have overpaid against. Paying more than rivals is a fact about the other bidders, not about the object's worth.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the version of the idea in general circulation, and the third paragraph states it in almost these words while describing its spread.

distractors.why_wrong: The account is arithmetical and turns on a scatter of honest estimates, so a perfectly calm bidder who submits an unadjusted estimate is exposed exactly as much as an excited one. The passage's own remedy is a subtraction rather than a change of mood.
distractors.seductive_element: The resentful bidders of the third paragraph keep temperament in the reader's mind, and the everyday version of the idea is about getting carried away.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage lists three conditions and shows the result vanishing when the first is absent, so the appointment of a highest-rated candidate establishes nothing until the value is known to be one quantity common to all the raters. Asserting the curse wherever a contest is decided is precisely the travelled habit the last paragraph calls useless.
distractors.seductive_element: Hiring looks structurally identical to bidding, and the passage's own list of take-overs and transfer fees invites the reader to add another case.

vocabulary.passage_use: shade the bid below the estimate
vocabulary.meaning_here: to reduce a figure slightly and deliberately

vocabulary.passage_use: when the dispersion of their estimates is wide
vocabulary.meaning_here: how widely a set of values is spread around its centre

vocabulary.passage_use: where it hardened into a maxim
vocabulary.meaning_here: a short general saying offered as a rule of conduct

mentor.challenge: An idea is followed from the place it was discovered to the place it is now quoted. Keep asking which version of it a sentence is about, because the passage's verdict on the two is opposite.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The winner's curse was an explanation of one arrangement, a value common to all bidders, honest estimates erring in both directions, and an award to the highest number, and the version now in circulation keeps the warning while losing the conditions, becoming a saying that no outcome can contradict.
mentor.main_idea: An oil company found that the tracts it won returned less than its geologists had predicted, and the explanation was arithmetic rather than psychological: the auction hands the tract to whichever firm overestimated it most. The cure is to subtract before bidding. As the idea spread it kept the warning and dropped the three conditions it needs, and in that form it explains every outcome and guides nobody.
mentor.simple_explanation:
An oil company noticed a pattern: the pieces of seabed it won at auction were worth less than its own experts had predicted. The experts were not bad at their jobs. Their guesses about the tracts the company lost were just as good, and overall their errors were as often too low as too high.

Here is the answer. Imagine several firms guessing the value of the same piece of ground. The true value is one number, and everyone's guess is a bit off in one direction or the other. Now, who wins the auction? Not an average guesser. The firm that guessed highest. And guessing highest usually means being the most wrong in the upward direction. So the winner is picked out for being too optimistic, without anybody being foolish.

The fix is simple arithmetic: bid a bit less than your estimate, and take off more when there are lots of bidders or when everyone's guesses are far apart.

Bidders hated this at first because it sounded like an insult. Then it became standard. Then the phrase escaped. Now people say 'the winner's curse' about take-overs, footballers, book deals and executive pay.

But the original idea only works if three things are true: the thing has one value that is the same for everybody, the guesses are wrong in both directions, and the prize goes to the highest number. Take away the first and it collapses. At a charity auction, a signed book is worth different amounts to different people, so the person who pays most simply wanted it most. He has not overpaid for anything.

And even with all three conditions, the curse is avoidable: subtract properly and you can win and still get a bargain.

So the popular version is empty. If you lose money you were cursed, if you make money you were lucky, and if you walk away you were wise. Nothing could ever prove it wrong, which is another way of saying it never tells you what to do. The narrow version does tell you: check three conditions, then subtract.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage asks the reader to hold two versions of one idea apart for five paragraphs, and the words for them are the same. Its central mechanism is statistical rather than psychological, which cuts against the explanation most readers arrive with, and the text refuses that explanation twice without ever naming it. The fourth paragraph then performs three separate removals in quick succession, and two of the four questions are built on them. Finally, the criticism in the last paragraph is not that the popular maxim is false but that nothing could make it false, which is a harder charge to keep hold of than simple error.
mentor.author_intention: To show that what makes an idea quotable and what makes it usable can be different parts of it, and to hand back the conditions that were dropped on the way to the saying.

paragraph_journey.note: An oil firm's winning leases kept underperforming its own forecasts, and neither incompetence nor systematic over-optimism explained it.
An auction sells to the highest guesser, who is usually the most wrong upward. Nobody is foolish, and the cure is to subtract before bidding.
Bidders resented it, then adopted it, and then the phrase escaped into general talk about take-overs, transfers and pay.
The account needs three conditions. Take away the common value, as at a charity auction, and there is nothing left to have overpaid against.
The travelled version fits every outcome and so advises nobody. The narrow one names conditions you can check and an amount to take off.

mentor.tone_progression: Neutral and narrative while the anomaly and its explanation are set out, faintly amused at the resentment of the bidders and the escape of the phrase, and severe at the close, where a popular saying is judged not false but empty.
key_transitions: 'The account that survived is arithmetical and says nothing about character.' (paragraph 2): the explanation is separated from blame.
'What travelled was the warning. What stayed behind were the conditions.' (paragraph 4): the sentence the whole passage is organised around.
'A warning nobody can fail to satisfy tells nobody what to do.' (paragraph 5): the charge against the popular version, which is emptiness rather than error.
mentor.misunderstanding: Most readers arrive with the everyday version of the idea, in which people get carried away and pay too much, and the passage never contradicts it in so many words. It contradicts it structurally: the errors run in both directions, the explanation is called arithmetical, and the remedy is a subtraction that a calm bidder and an excited one can perform equally well. A second misreading takes the passage for a general law about winners, which the charity book and the closing paragraph both refuse.
mentor.traps_summary: The distractors are built from the two familiar versions of the idea, overpaying is what winning means, and bidders get carried away, and from the generalisation the passage spends a paragraph withdrawing. Each is stated in language the passage itself uses. When an essay traces an idea's history, ask of every option which stage of the history it belongs to.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage gives an explanation together with the conditions it requires, treat those conditions as the answer key for the whole set. Questions about purpose, assumption, comparison and inference will all turn on whether an option keeps the conditions or drops them, and the most attractive wrong answers are the ones that keep the conclusion while quietly leaving a condition behind.
mentor.real_world: The same discipline applies whenever a striking finding reaches ordinary conversation: nudges, placebo effects, survivorship bias. Each began with a setting and a set of conditions, and each is now applied to cases in which somebody would have to check first.
mentor.takeaway: An idea that explains every outcome has stopped being able to advise anybody.
mentor.reflection_question: Which of the ideas you quote most confidently could you still state together with the conditions under which it holds?

eli10.big_idea: The idea that auction winners overpay holds only under three conditions; the popular saying dropped them, so it fits everything and helps nobody.
eli10.story: The land an oil company won at auction kept earning less than its experts forecast. The experts were not bad; their errors ran both ways. Picture ten friends guessing the sweets in one jar. Some guess high, some low. Now each bids their guess, and the top bid wins. The winner is the one who guessed furthest too high. Nobody is foolish. The fix: bid a little below your guess. Later the idea escaped into everyday talk as 'the winner overpaid'. But it needs three things: one true value for everyone, guesses wrong both ways, and the top bid winning. A signed book at a charity sale has no single value. Paying most just means wanting it most. Even with all three, a bidder who takes some off can win a bargain. The popular saying fits every result, so it helps nobody; the original tells you what to check.
paragraphs: Starts with a puzzle: land an oil firm won kept disappointing, though its experts were sound.
Explains it: the auction picks the highest guess, the one most wrong upwards, so bid below your estimate.
Tells how the idea was resented, then accepted, then turned into a saying used everywhere.
Lists the three conditions the saying lost, and shows that even with all three, overpaying is avoidable.
Judges the saying: it fits every outcome, so it guides nobody, while the narrow version can be checked.
eli10.author_view: Firm and a little stern: the writer admires the careful original idea and thinks the popular saying is empty.
